title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
abstract: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval).

title: About the Alignment Science Blog
abstract: We are Anthropic'sAlignment Science team. We do machine learning research on the problem of steering and controlling future powerful AI systems, as well as understanding and evaluating the risks that they pose. Welcome to our blog! This blog is inspired by the informal updates on our Interpretability team'sTransformer Circuits thread. We'll use it to release research notes and early findings that we don't think warrant a full publication, but might nonetheless be useful to others working on similar problems. P.S.we're hiring!

title: Managing Biological Risks from General-Purpose AI Models under the EU AI Act
abstract: Recommendations to strengthen how developers of advanced AI models assess, mitigate, and report biological risks under the EU AI Act. An intelligence explosion would compress years of progress into months and create urgent challenges for oversight, control, and governance. Embedded assessments can enable deeper and more flexible assessments of risks that depend on internal systems and practices. How to ensure AI safety incidents are identified, investigated, and used to improve safety across the industry. Developers rely on model-level, deployment-level, and governance-level interventions to address extreme misuse risks. Policymakers should complement biosecurity measures with stronger biosafety systems. As AI agents make government services easier to access, governments need to balance measures against surges in demand against the risk of reducing equitable access. The US military faces organizational, technical, and operational barriers to adopting AI at scale.

title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
abstract: Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly. Unfortunately, as discussed , there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours.

title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
abstract: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge A key problem in AI safety is eliciting latent knowledge (ELK), extracting information from a model that is misaligned and more knowledgeable than its overseer. For example, a misaligned model used to scan code for vulnerabilities may want to withhold its findings, i.e., sandbag, in order to exploit them later. To study ELK empirically, we need model organisms that mirror this setting. Existing model organisms fall short in several respects. In this work, we train model organisms to withhold solutions in a vulnerability detection task.

title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
abstract: TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. Minimal Viable Safety The Task The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do . For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless. We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger.

title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
abstract: Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations. Introduction Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is . Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
abstract: Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557 Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate , which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box.

title: “Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming” by Gosha Kozhevnikov, Tyler
abstract: Subtitle: Automatically finding monitor failures by editing real agent transcripts. We introduce Screwtape, a pipeline that turns agent transcripts into realistic attacks that evade action-only monitors (monitors that don’t look at the agent's chain of thought) by inserting an attack into a transcript and repeatedly refining it until a monitor no longer catches it. An LLM verifier with access to the edited transcript and an attack description checks whether the attack is realistic, is clearly harmful, and could plausibly succeed in the original environment. We ran the pipeline on Redwood staff transcripts with our own monitors based on Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, and then tested the resulting attacks against a held-out monitor from a frontier developer. We ran the pipeline 252 times on 94 unique transcripts. This produced 35 attacks that evaded our monitors.

title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
abstract: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] .

title: A Pre-mortem on The First Major AI-Enabled Terrorism Event and The Choices That Could Enable it: Plus 9 Predictions
abstract: A Pre-mortem on The First Major AI-Enabled Terrorism Event and The Choices That Could Enable it: Plus 9 Predictions Frontier AI developers' model reports and the dedicated risk-assessment teams at governmental AI institutes such as UK AISI and US CAISSI now treat a major AI-enabled cyber, biological, or chemical terror event as a credible concern. But how, precisely, might such an event happen? What choices across the model lifecycle may contribute to it? This paper studies what current evidence suggests about how specific mistakes from AI developers, distributors, and governments may contribute to such an event. ​ The authors conclude with a set of 9 falsifiable predictions about how the first major AI-enabled cyber, bio, or chemical terrorism attack may occur and outline two illustrative hypothetical scenarios for such an event.
